one_liner: Entry-level CIA operations officer trained to recruit and handle foreign sources overseas, spending most of a career on multi-year assignments abroad.
fit_summary: Daniel's relationship-building, comfort with people, and deep knowledge of U.S. policy match the core of this role, which centers on building rapport and assessing character and motivation. But the job means a career mostly overseas, a Top Secret/SCI background investigation with polygraph, a 5-year contract term, and worldwide medical clearance, which is a different path than the domestic government career Daniel described. It is also unclear whether Daniel holds the required bachelor's degree.
eligibility: U.S. citizenship and the ability to pass a CIA background investigation for Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access are required.
A bachelor's degree from an accredited institution is required (or within one year of earning one); a 3.0 GPA is preferred, and foreign degrees need a credential evaluation.
You must be medically clearable for worldwide deployment and meet the listed physical tasks, such as driving day and night and traversing uneven terrain.
Placement depends on experience: Clandestine Service Trainee (CST) with three or more years of professional experience, or Professional Trainee (PT) with less.
You must sign a 5-year Contract Term Agreement; the posting is open to the public, so federal status is not needed.
keywords: spot, assess, develop, recruit, and handle
build relationships based on rapport and trust
work effectively as part of a team and independently
make reasoned decisions under time constraints
strategy: Decide first whether a mostly overseas, multi-year-assignment career fits your goals. If you prefer a domestic, policy, or legislative role, put your energy elsewhere or look at other CIA directorates.

Apply through cia.gov/careers as the posting directs, not by relying only on USAJOBS. The window runs Sept 1, 2026 to Jan 31, 2027, but apply early because the security process can take a year or more.

Frame your IEM work around client relationship management, working with government stakeholders, judgment under deadline pressure during disasters, and adapting to fast-changing situations. Stick to what you actually did.
Count your years of professional experience carefully to see whether you qualify for CST (3+ years) or PT, and state your dates clearly.
Highlight any foreign language study, international travel, or cultural exposure, plus your policy knowledge as it relates to national security issues.
Keep a clean, honest record of your history for the SF-86, including residences, foreign contacts, drug use, and finances. Avoid publicizing your application or discussing it on social media.
resume_bullets: Built and maintained working relationships with [number/type of] government client stakeholders at IEM, earning trust to [describe outcome you can verify] on [emergency management/recovery project].
Made reasoned decisions under time constraints during [specific disaster response or exercise], coordinating [number] team members and partners to deliver [deliverable] by [deadline].
Researched and briefed [audience] on [policy/national security topic], translating complex information into clear written and verbal products used for [purpose].
interview_questions: Tell us about a time you built trust with someone quickly who was initially skeptical or guarded.
Describe a situation where you had to make a decision with incomplete information under time pressure.
How do you assess what motivates another person? Give an example.
How would you and your family handle years of overseas assignments and erratic schedules?
watch_outs: The security clearance process with polygraph is long and invasive, and past drug use, finances, or foreign ties can disqualify you or delay you.
Most of the career is spent overseas, with no telework and a 5-year contract term. That is a major lifestyle commitment.
A bachelor's degree is mandatory; confirm Daniel has one or will finish within a year.
Applications and status are confidential, so keep the process discreet and expect little feedback.
